newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sets date to hand back Chinese hijackers.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sets date to hand back Chinese hijackers.

text.p: Taiwan soon will repatriate two mainland hijackers who commandeered Chinese jetliners to Taiwan, reciprocating for Beijing's unprecedented handover of a Taiwan hijacker in May, state media said on Thursday.

Taipei's semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation and Red Cross officials in the nearby mainland province of Fujian would handle the repatriation of Han Fengying and Huang Shugang on July 16, Taiwan's state-funded Central News Agency said.
Han and Huang have served four-year prison terms for air piracy on the island, which has been estranged from the Chinese mainland since a 1949 civil war split.
In a letter to the Red Cross, the Taipei foundation urged the mainland side to adhere to the principles of humanity, security and convenience when handling the case.
The Straits Exchange Foundation handles talks between the long-time rivals in the absence of official contacts.
The hijackers would be transferred by sea from Taiwan's front-line island of Quemoy, also called Jinmen, to Fujian.
Taiwan officials were unavailable for comment.
Han and Huang may face new trials in China on air piracy charges, a capital offence in the communist mainland.
Despite completing their prison terms, the two remain illegal aliens in Taiwan and have been held in a special centre for mainlanders who entered the island without documents.
Including Han and Huang, Taiwan currently holds 16 mainlanders who hijacked 12 planes to Taiwan in 1993-1994 before China tightened airport security.

Taiwan itself helped curb the tide of hijackings from the mainland by putting air pirates on trial and imprisoning them, a major shift from earlier decades when hijackers were hailed as anti-Communist freedom fighters.
Beijing also has shifted policy, returning Taiwan hijacker Liu Shan-chung in May rather than letting him stay on and giving him a job, as it did with an earlier Taiwan air pirate.
That handover marked the first hijacker repatriation across the Taiwan strait and was completed despite the absence of a formal repatriation pact.
Taiwan and China, which have no formal links since the 1949 split, reached consensus on hijacker repatriation in 1995 but did not sign the accord due to subsequent political frictions.
Beijing froze bilateral negotiations 24 months ago to protest a landmark private visit to the United States by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui in mid-1995.
Beijing has consistently declined Taipei's call to resume semi-official talks, saying no dialogue would be possible until Taiwan agreed to stop engaging in what China called "splittist" activities.
